figs.fig-beeformer:
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 450" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif">
  <rect width="800" height="450" rx="14" fill="#FAFAF7" stroke="#E5E7EB"/>
  <defs>
    <marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10" fill="#6B7280"/>
    </marker>
    <marker id="g" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10" fill="#7C3AED"/>
    </marker>
    <style>
      .gradient-flow{animation:back 6s ease-in-out infinite}
      .encoder-update{animation:learn 6s ease-in-out infinite}
      @keyframes back{
        0%,18%{stroke-dashoffset:0}
        52%,88%{stroke-dashoffset:-84}
        100%{stroke-dashoffset:-108}
      }
      @keyframes learn{
        0%,42%{fill:#E0F2FE}
        58%,88%{fill:#D1FAE5}
        100%{fill:#E0F2FE}
      }
    </style>
  </defs>

  <text x="400" y="34" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" font-weight="700" fill="#1E1B4B">beeFormer: Let Recommendation Loss Reach Text</text>

  <rect class="encoder-update" x="70" y="120" width="190" height="78" rx="10" fill="#E0F2FE" stroke="#075985" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="165" y="150" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" fill="#075985">
    <tspan x="165" font-weight="700">Sentence transformer</tspan>
    <tspan x="165" dy="21">text encoder</tspan>
  </text>

  <rect x="335" y="120" width="130" height="78" rx="10" fill="#D1FAE5" stroke="#065F46" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="400" y="150" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" fill="#065F46">
    <tspan x="400" font-weight="700">Item vectors</tspan>
    <tspan x="400" dy="21">text + behaviour</tspan>
  </text>

  <rect x="540" y="120" width="190" height="78" rx="10" fill="#EDE9FE" stroke="#4C1D95" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="635" y="150" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" fill="#4C1D95">
    <tspan x="635" font-weight="700">ELSA</tspan>
    <tspan x="635" dy="21">collaborative objective</tspan>
  </text>

  <path d="M260 159 H335" fill="none" stroke="#6B7280" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/>
  <text x="297" y="107" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6B7280">encodes items</text>

  <path d="M465 159 H540" fill="none" stroke="#6B7280" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/>
  <text x="503" y="107" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6B7280">feeds vectors</text>

  <path class="gradient-flow" d="M635 198 C635 274 165 274 165 198" fill="none" stroke="#7C3AED" stroke-width="4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-dasharray="14 9" marker-end="url(#g)"/>
  <text x="400" y="288" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#4C1D95">ELSA recommendation gradient updates the encoder</text>

  <rect x="70" y="312" width="300" height="68" rx="10" fill="#FEE2E2" stroke="#991B1B" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="220" y="339" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" fill="#991B1B">
    <tspan x="220" font-weight="700">Standard practice: encoder frozen</tspan>
    <tspan x="220" dy="21" fill="#6B7280">recommender loss cannot teach the text model</tspan>
  </text>

  <rect x="430" y="312" width="300" height="68" rx="10" fill="#D1FAE5" stroke="#065F46" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="580" y="339" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" fill="#065F46">
    <tspan x="580" font-weight="700">Cross-domain transfer</tspan>
    <tspan x="580" dy="21">train on books → recommend films</tspan>
  </text>

  <text x="400" y="428" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" fill="#6B7280">Collaborative loss teaches the text encoder which meanings predict what users choose.</text>
</svg>

  <rect x="530" y="288" width="238" height="98" rx="10" fill="#E0F2FE" stroke="#075985" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="649" y="309" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1E1B4B" font-size="11">

    <tspan x="649" dy="20">Repsys</tspan>
    <tspan x="649" dy="17">offline-online bridging</tspan>
    <tspan x="649" dy="17">uncertainty estimation</tspan>
  </text>

  <g fill="none" stroke="#6B7280" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linecap="round" marker-end="url(#a)">
    <path class="thread" d="M270 135 C282 145 291 160 310 178"/>
    <path class="thread t2" d="M530 135 C518 145 509 160 490 178"/>
    <path class="thread t3" d="M530 337 C518 327 509 297 490 276"/>
    <path class="thread t4" d="M270 337 C282 327 291 297 310 276"/>
  </g>

  <rect x="286" y="174" width="228" height="106" rx="10" fill="#D1FAE5" stroke="#065F46" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="400" y="197" text-anchor="middle" fill="#065F46">
    <tspan x="400" font-size="11" font-weight="700">SHARED QUESTION</tspan>
    <tspan x="400" dy="23" font-size="12.5" fill="#1E1B4B">How do we put</tspan>
    <tspan x="400" dy="21" font-size="15" font-weight="700">large-model quality</tspan>
    <tspan x="400" dy="21" font-size="12.5" fill="#1E1B4B">inside an ordinary budget?</tspan>
  </text>

  <text x="400" y="428" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" fill="#6B7280">Every publication asks how to fit large-model quality into a budget someone will approve.</text>

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 880 500" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif">
  <rect width="880" height="500" rx="18" fill="#FAFAF7" stroke="#E5E7EB"/>
  <text x="440" y="43" text-anchor="middle" font-size="22" font-weight="700" fill="#1E1B4B">Same catalogue. Different growth curve.</text>
  <text x="440" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" fill="#6B7280">Illustrative model-parameter storage · 10M items · float32</text>

  <rect x="42" y="110" width="373" height="286" rx="16" fill="#FFF1F2" stroke="#FDA4AF" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="72" y="151" font-size="24" font-weight="700" fill="#9F1239">EASE</text>
  <text x="72" y="181" font-size="15" fill="#881337">every item stores a weight for every item</text>
  <rect x="72" y="211" width="313" height="85" rx="10" fill="#FFE4E6"/>
  <text x="228" y="248" text-anchor="middle" font-size="25" font-weight="700" fill="#9F1239">I × I</text>
  <text x="228" y="274" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" fill="#881337">quadratic parameter matrix</text>
  <text x="72" y="337" font-size="16" fill="#4C0519">10M × 10M × 4 bytes</text>
  <text x="72" y="374" font-size="30" font-weight="800" fill="#9F1239">≈ 400 TB</text>

  <rect x="465" y="110" width="373" height="286" rx="16" fill="#ECFDF5" stroke="#6EE7B7" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="495" y="151" font-size="24" font-weight="700" fill="#065F46">ELSA</text>
  <text x="495" y="181" font-size="15" fill="#047857">every item stores a fixed-width embedding</text>
  <rect x="495" y="211" width="313" height="85" rx="10" fill="#D1FAE5"/>
  <text x="651" y="248" text-anchor="middle" font-size="25" font-weight="700" fill="#065F46">I × 512</text>

  <text x="495" y="337" font-size="16" fill="#064E3B">10M × 512 × 4 bytes</text>

  <text x="440" y="473" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" font-weight="600" fill="#374151">The baseline stays useful only if it fits the catalogue.</text>
</svg>

figs.fig-feedback-loop:
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 450" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif">
  <rect width="800" height="450" rx="14" fill="#FAFAF7" stroke="#E5E7EB"/>
  <defs>
    <marker id="a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10" fill="#6B7280"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <style>
    @keyframes flow {
      0%, 18% { stroke-dashoffset: 0; }
      82%, 100% { stroke-dashoffset: -48; }
    }
    .flow {
      animation: flow 6s ease-in-out infinite;
    }
  </style>

  <text x="400" y="34" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" font-weight="700" fill="#1E1B4B">The model learns only from what it showed</text>

  <path class="flow" d="M465 86 C510 86 530 127 575 127
                         M650 149 C650 180 680 195 680 235
                         M610 257 C580 290 550 320 500 334
                         M430 356 C385 356 370 297 345 297
                         M205 297 C160 220 215 86 335 86"
        fill="none" stroke="#EF4444" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="7 5"
        stroke-linecap="round" marker-end="url(#a)"/>

  <rect x="335" y="64" width="130" height="44" rx="10" fill="#FEE2E2" stroke="#991B1B" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="400" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#991B1B">Model</text>

  <rect x="575" y="105" width="150" height="44" rx="10" fill="#FEE2E2" stroke="#991B1B" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="650" y="133" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#991B1B">Chooses what to show</text>

  <rect x="610" y="235" width="140" height="44" rx="10" fill="#FEE2E2" stroke="#991B1B" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="680" y="263" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#991B1B">User reacts</text>

  <rect x="430" y="334" width="120" height="44" rx="10" fill="#FEE2E2" stroke="#991B1B" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="490" y="362" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#991B1B">Interaction log</text>

  <rect x="205" y="275" width="140" height="44" rx="10" fill="#FEE2E2" stroke="#991B1B" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="275" y="303" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#991B1B">Training</text>

  <text x="520" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#991B1B">scores candidates</text>
  <text x="735" y="194" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#991B1B">exposes items</text>
  <text x="598" y="307" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#991B1B">click / skip</text>
  <text x="384" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#991B1B">becomes data</text>
  <text x="264" y="249" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#991B1B">updates model</text>

  <text x="435" y="168" text-anchor="middle" fill="#991B1B">
    <tspan x="435" font-size="11" font-weight="700">CONSEQUENCES</tspan>
    <tspan x="435" y="194" font-size="12.5">• Unobserved is not negative</tspan>
    <tspan x="435" y="221" font-size="12.5">• Offline metrics inherit the bias</tspan>
    <tspan x="435" y="248" font-size="12.5">• The loop self-reinforces</tspan>
  </text>

  <path d="M50 120 H134 Q140 120 140 126 V138 Q140 144 134 144 H50 Q44 144 44 138 V126 Q44 120 50 120 Z
           M50 155 H134 Q140 155 140 161 V173 Q140 179 134 179 H50 Q44 179 44 173 V161 Q44 155 50 155 Z
           M50 190 H134 Q140 190 140 196 V208 Q140 214 134 214 H50 Q44 214 44 208 V196 Q44 190 50 190 Z"
        fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#E5E7EB" stroke-width="2" opacity="0.7"/>

  <text x="92" y="101" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7280" opacity="0.72">
    <tspan x="92" font-size="11" font-weight="700">ITEMS NEVER SHOWN</tspan>
    <tspan x="92" y="137" font-size="11">item A</tspan>
    <tspan x="92" y="172" font-size="11">item B</tspan>
    <tspan x="92" y="207" font-size="11">item C</tspan>
    <tspan x="92" y="237" font-size="11">no exposure, no feedback</tspan>
  </text>

  <text x="400" y="428" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" fill="#6B7280">The model never sees feedback on what it did not show, and neither does your metric.</text>
</svg>

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 450" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif">

  <rect x="40" y="67" width="720" height="312" rx="10" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#E5E7EB" stroke-width="2"/>
  <path d="M40 111H760 M40 178H760 M40 245H760 M40 312H760 M160 67V379 M550 67V379" fill="none" stroke="#E5E7EB" stroke-width="2"/>

  <g class="effect-focus">
    <rect x="562" y="121" width="186" height="47" rx="10" fill="#FEF3C7" stroke="#92400E" stroke-width="2"/>
  </g>

  <text x="100" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#6B7280">SYSTEM</text>
  <text x="355" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#6B7280">SERVING TRICK</text>
  <text x="655" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#6B7280">MEASURED EFFECT</text>

  <text x="100" y="149" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#4C1D95">PinFM</text>
  <text x="355" y="149" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" fill="#92400E">deduplicated cross-attention (DCAT)</text>
  <text x="655" y="149" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#92400E">+600% throughput</text>

  <text x="100" y="216" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#4C1D95">UniPinRec</text>
  <text x="355" y="216" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" fill="#92400E">KV-cache reuse + FP8 + flex attention</text>
  <text x="655" y="216" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" font-weight="700" fill="#92400E">3.92× faster ranking forward pass</text>

  <text x="100" y="283" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#4C1D95">GEMs</text>
  <text x="355" y="283" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" fill="#92400E">multi-stream decoder</text>
  <text x="655" y="283" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#92400E">−70% latency</text>

  <text x="100" y="350" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#4C1D95">YouTube</text>
  <text x="355" y="350" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" fill="#92400E">quantisation + distillation</text>
  <text x="655" y="350" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#92400E">~20% faster inference</text>

  <text x="400" y="428" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" fill="#6B7280">PinFM's +600% throughput came from an attention trick omitted from the abstract.</text>
</svg>

slides.body:
**Classical retrieval: BM25 + cosine similarity**

![[fig-bm25-cosine|105%]]

`score(q,d) = α · BM25(q,d) + (1 − α) · cosine(q,d)`, with hand-set `α ∈ [0,1]`.

> Pointwise linear regression learns feature weights; it cannot rerank documents omitted from the BM25 top-*k* set.

<!-- col -->

**Pointwise learning to rank: linear regression**

![[fig-pointwise-linear-regression]]

`ŷ(q,d) = w₀ + Σᵢ wᵢxᵢ(q,d)`; fit `w` from query–document relevance labels using squared error.

<!-- col -->

| | Classical | Pointwise LTR |
|---|---|---|
| Inputs | BM25 and cosine similarity | BM25, cosine similarity, and other query–document features |
| Weights | Hand-set `α` | Learned coefficients `wᵢ` |
| Output | Combined similarity score | Predicted relevance `ŷ(q,d)` |
| Scope | Retrieves and sorts documents | Reranks the BM25 top-*k* candidates |
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:05:30 · 2 min — Two stages: a cheap filter that must not miss, a learned ranker that orders. Trace the two columns, then the last line: a reranker cannot rescue what the first stage dropped.

slides.body:
**Scoring function**

`linear regression` → `regression trees (LambdaMART)` → `neural ranker`

<!-- gap -->

| Training objective | Training data | What it learns |
|---|---|---|
| **Itemwise cross-entropy** | `(query, document, relevant?)` | 1 relevance probability: `−y log p − (1−y) log(1−p)` |
| **Pairwise loss (RankNet)** | `(query, preferred doc, other doc)` | 1 score difference: `log(1 + exp(−(s⁺−s⁻)))` |
| **Listwise loss (ListNet)** | 1 query, its candidate list and graded labels | A distribution over the list via softmax cross-entropy |

**Pairwise loss computation — 4 animation steps**

`D⁺: "Noise-cancelling headphones, 30-hour battery"` → `D⁻: "Replacement headphone cable"` → `(D⁺, D⁻)` → `s⁺=1.2, s⁻=0.4` → `loss=log(1+exp(−0.8))=0.371`

<!-- col -->

![[fig-pairwise-loss-computation]]

> One pair supervises 1 score difference between 2 documents; it does not identify absolute relevance probabilities.

slides.body:
- A recommender stores embeddings of users and items
- This research prototype maps a natural language sentence into a change in the user embedding space
- The existing recommender produces a new ranking without retraining or reranking at request time

![[fig-steering-pipeline|85%]]

**Offline example:** the rank of item relevant to the steering sentence improved from 10th to 5th on average using MIND dataset and ALS as CF backbone

> Jarda Hradil · MSc thesis, 2026 · experimental
slides.notes:
The core question we’ve had - could we allow steering recommendations using natural language without some expensive reranking?

And the answer is yes -pretty much every recommender stores embeddings of users and items and calculates the predicted interaction as their dot product. If we project the dense embeddings of users into sparse latent space and then learn mapping from item metadata to the sparse latent space, we are then able to take a user’s natural language request, map it to a meaningful change in the sparse embedding, and decode it to obtain manipulated user embedding. When we calculate the dot product of this manipulated embedding with item embeddings, it will score higher the items that are relevant to the natural language request without adding explicit reranking step.

So for example a user with interaction history that reflects a profile of someone interested in politics and finance can type “I want to see more tour de france news” and the mapper will translate this into increasing a specific neuron activation in the sparse latent space, which after decoding will result in tour de france news getting naturally blended into politics and finance recommendations.
slides.title: Research preview: steer recommendations with a sentence (Jarda)
slides.summary: Hradil 2026, part one: a TopK sparse autoencoder projects the dense CF user embedding into a wide latent where most features mean one thing.

<!-- col -->

**Illustrative scale scenario—not a vendor quote**

100 M users × 3 sessions/day × 5 pages
= **1.5 billion ranking calls/day**

At **~10,000 tokens/call** (prompt + query + candidate documents) and a measured **~$0.08/million tokens** (GPU cost ÷ throughput):

**~$1.2 million/day** for the LLM step alone, before retrieval and without caching.

<!-- gap -->

| Constraint | Implication |
|---|---|
| Example recommendation budget: **≈100 ms** end-to-end | Every component shares the latency budget |
| Kuaishou reports **>400,000 requests/s, <500 ms** ([OneRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13695)) | Architecture matters at scale |

**Limit:** this is the uncached, unbatched cost of a generic LLM — at a fraction of this traffic, or with the tricks on the next slide, the bill drops by orders of magnitude, not just a little.

> Use generation where it adds value—not automatically on every page view.
slides.notes:
The token count and the price are both measured now, not a vendor quote or a guess: ~10,000 tokens/call is a typical candidate set run through our own truncator's token-estimation convention, plus the system prompt and instructions any LLM-as-ranker needs. The ~$0.08/M-token price comes from a $200/month GPU divided by its actual average throughput, not a price list. Actual bills still depend on model, token mix and caching — redo the arithmetic at your own traffic and compare cost per successful customer outcome.

⏱ 9:31 · 1½ min — One line of arithmetic: 1.5 billion ranking calls a day; a language model on that path is about $1.2 million a day before caching; a dot product is microseconds. Cost per request is an objective, not an ops detail.
slides.title: Would you put an LLM on every ranking request? (Dan)
slides.summary: Q6 opener: the budget nobody negotiates — QPS, latency, and the fact that a recommender request is a dot product while a language-model request is thousands of tokens.

slides.body:
![[fig-dan-serving-path]]

<!-- col -->

<!-- gap -->

> 1.5 billion requests a day are not 1.5 billion different questions.

| Stage | Budget | What we do about it |
|---|---|---|
| Retrieval | ~40 ms | hybrid vector + keyword search over the catalog |
| Ranking | ~60 ms | semantic cache first; GPU cluster only on a miss |
| Assembly | negligible | merge + threshold |

- **The trick that paid off most:** query traffic follows a classic Zipf distribution — a small head of intents covers most of the volume — so a semantic cache keyed on intent turns most requests into a lookup, not a GPU call. Millions of cached results fit into a few gigabytes of memory; only genuine misses reach the GPU cluster, split by document length and scored in parallel.
- **What it costs to keep:** the GPU cluster itself — today's GPU prices aren't small — plus load balancing and failover, since one worker dropping mid-request can't stall the response.
- **Limit:** the cache only works because traffic is skewed. Cold-start and long-tail queries have no skew to exploit — they hit the GPU cluster every time, and that fleet, not the cache, is the real fixed cost behind the 100 ms number.
slides.notes:
This is the other half of the arithmetic: where the 100 ms budget from the previous slide actually goes, and the one thing that keeps it affordable. Retrieval takes about 40 ms, ranking about 60 ms; assembly is noise.

1.5 billion requests a day sounds like enormous diversity, but it isn't — query frequency follows a classic Zipf distribution, so a small head of intents covers most of the volume. We cache on that intent, not the exact text, so near-duplicate searches share a cached ranking instead of paying for a fresh GPU pass every time. Only real misses — after a combined vector-and-keyword retrieval pass — reach the GPU cluster, and even those get split across workers and scored in parallel.

That only works because of the skew, and the skew runs out: cold-start and long-tail queries have nothing to cache against, so they hit the GPU cluster every single time. That cluster — GPU capacity, load balancing, failover for a worker dropping mid-request — is the real fixed cost behind the 100 ms number, not the cache.

Retrieval has its own limit worth a one-liner if asked: a lightweight ANN index can miss recall and need a bigger graph before it holds up, and exact search only stays practical on a small catalogue — it doesn't scale to ours.
slides.title: Where the milliseconds and the money actually go (Dan)
slides.summary: Companion to 14: where the 100ms budget goes, and how a Zipf-skewed semantic cache keeps most requests off the GPU cluster.

| **Kuaishou OneRec:** App Stay Time **+0.54% / +1.24%**, with roughly **10×** the arithmetic of its previous cascade | More computation need not mean proportionally higher serving cost |

[HSTU, 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152) · [OneRec, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13695)

![[fig-serving-tricks|140%]]

<!-- col -->

| Practical lever | Reported example |
|---|---|
| **Cache customer state** | MTServe: up to **3.1×** faster |
| **Share work between retrieval and ranking** | UniPinRec: **−11.1%** latency |
| **Avoid repeatedly processing the same history** | PinFM: **+600%** serving throughput |
| **Process long histories more efficiently** | Douyin: **−77–84%** bandwidth |

[MTServe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.22881) · [UniPinRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00422) · [PinFM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12704) · [Douyin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.06077)

> Different systems and baselines: these gains are not additive.

slides.title: Four ways to avoid paying for the same work twice
slides.summary: Q7: the tricks that make long histories and big models fit the budget — caches across requests, reuse across stages, deduplicated attention, linear attention with request-level batching.

slides.body:
![[fig-ease-vs-elsa|135%]]

<!-- col -->

> Keep the baseline; make its footprint grow with the catalogue, not its square.

| EASE | ELSA |
|---|---|
| Item-item weights: **I × I** | Item embeddings: **I × d** |
| Storage grows **quadratically** | Storage grows **linearly** |
| Strong simple baseline | Practical beyond roughly **20k items** |

- Comparable offline quality to EASE; reported online tests were consistently better.
- **Sparse ELSA (2026):** **10×** smaller embeddings with no reported accuracy loss; **100×** smaller with **2.5%** loss.

[ELSA, RecSys 2022](https://doi.org/10.1145/3523227.3551482) · [Large-scale evaluation, 2025](https://doi.org/10.1145/3748335) · [Sparse ELSA, WWW 2026](https://doi.org/10.1145/3774904.3792914)
slides.notes:
The numbers in the figure are illustrative storage arithmetic for model parameters only: 10 million squared float32 values are about 400 TB; 10 million × 512 float32 values are about 20.5 GB. They exclude optimizer state, index structures, replication and serving overhead.

⏱ 9:35 · 1½ min — EASE is the baseline to beat, but its item-item matrix becomes the product constraint. At ten million items, the uncompressed matrix is about 400 TB. ELSA represents every item with a fixed-width vector instead: at 512 dimensions, about 20 GB before operational overhead. The threshold is not universal — catalogue sparsity, hardware and latency decide it — but the 2022 results found ELSA beneficial beyond roughly 20k items. The follow-up work asks how much farther we can compress those embeddings before quality moves: 10× smaller without reported loss, 100× smaller for a 2.5% loss. Keep a serious baseline that fits the system, then demand that more complex models beat it on the outcome and the bill.
slides.title: ELSA makes a strong linear baseline scale (Vojta)
slides.summary: ELSA replaces EASE's quadratic item-item matrix with fixed-width item embeddings; later sparse ELSA pushes the storage-quality trade-off further.

slides.body:
> Sparse adapters beat both dense alternatives in 70 of 78 evaluation settings.

#### Semantic adapter

- **Frozen encoder:** BGE, Qwen3 or MiniLM
- **Training:** catalogue embeddings only
- **Interactions:** model selection and evaluation only
- **Representation:** top-k sparse code
- **Target:** held-out cold items

<!-- col -->

**13 datasets × 3 encoders × 2 metrics**

| Best adapter | Settings |
|---|---:|
| Denoising SAE | **46** |
| SAE | **24** |
| β-VAE | **8** |

Offline Recall@20 and NDCG@20

- **Compresso:** PyTorch `fit` / `transform`, fixed-k storage, clustering
- **Limit:** preliminary content-based evidence; no online, latency or cost result

[SAE adapters, RecSys 2026](https://doi.org/10.1145/3773078.3841253) · [Compresso, RecSys 2026](https://doi.org/10.1145/3773078.3841254)
slides.group: Our Transformers and multimodal foundational models
slides.notes:
The evaluation holds out items, not merely user interactions. The adapter sees the training catalogue's item-description embeddings and learns only to reconstruct them. Interactions appear in validation-based model selection and final evaluation, not in adapter training. The 78 settings are 13 datasets × 3 frozen embedding models × 2 offline metrics: Recall@20 and NDCG@20. D-SAE is best in 46 settings, SAE in 24 and β-VAE in 8. The paper states that the sparse variants beat both dense adapters in 70 of 78 settings. Do not present this as online lift or as a Compresso benchmark. Compresso is the open-source PyTorch framework that packages top-k SAE training, sparse row-packed storage, pruning and clustering.

⏱ 9:36:30 · 1½ min — Generic text embeddings know everything and therefore underrepresent distinctions that matter inside one catalogue. We freeze the encoder and train a small adapter only by reconstructing the catalogue embeddings. No interactions train it. On held-out cold items, sparse adapters beat both dense adapter variants in 70 of 78 combinations across 13 datasets, three encoders and two offline metrics. Compresso packages that workflow so the sparse codes can also be stored and inspected as domain factors. The limit matters: this is preliminary offline content-based evidence. We have not shown online lift, latency or serving cost here.
slides.title: Sparse adapters specialize generic item embeddings (Vojta)
slides.summary: Sparse autoencoder adapters learn domain-specific item features without interaction data during training; Compresso packages the sparse-learning workflow.

slides.body:
![[fig-beeformer|90%]]

<!-- col -->

> Projection learns around the encoder. beeFormer teaches the encoder what users choose.

- **Projection:** freeze the text model; map its embeddings into collaborative space
- **beeFormer:** use ELSA as the decoder; backpropagate interaction loss into the Transformer
- **Serving:** sentence embeddings and cosine similarity

| Offline Recall@20 | beeFormer | Best baseline |
|---|---:|---:|
| ML20M cold items | **0.4630** | 0.3204 · Heater |
| Amazon Books time split | **0.0706** | 0.0421 · SANSA |

**Limit:** no online, training-cost or latency result; item descriptions were Llama-generated.

[Paper](https://doi.org/10.1145/3640457.3691707) · [Code](https://github.com/recombee/beeformer)
slides.group: Our Transformers and multimodal foundational models
slides.notes: The design choice is where interaction supervision stops. In a projection model, the sentence Transformer remains generic and we learn a mapping from semantic to collaborative space. beeFormer replaces ELSA's free item matrix with embeddings produced by the Transformer, then lets ELSA's interaction reconstruction loss update the Transformer itself. In the offline experiments, Recall@20 on held-out MovieLens items was 0.4630 versus 0.3204 for the strongest Heater projection baseline. On the Amazon Books time split it was 0.0706 versus 0.0421 for SANSA. At serving time it is still a sentence encoder plus cosine similarity. The evidence is limited to offline tests: training cost and latency were not reported, and the standardized item descriptions were generated with Llama.
slides.title: beeFormer trains the text encoder on interaction loss (Vojta)

slides.body:
![[fig-winning-config]]

<!-- col -->

**REEF:** every encoder gets the same data, split, negatives and downstream ranker — only the encoder changes.

| Dataset | Recall@10, frozen → adapted | Cold start |
|---|---|---|
| MovieLens 20M | 0.301 → 0.349 (**+15.9%**) | 0.219 → 0.249 (**+13.7%**) |
| H&M Fashion | 0.164 → 0.211 (**+28.7%**) | 0.128 → 0.158 (**+23.4%**) |
| Amazon Reviews 2023 | 0.121 → 0.154 (**+27.3%**) | 0.100 → 0.139 (**+39.0%**) |

*BGE-M3 + SigLIP2 · offline · one target vs 999 sampled negatives*

- **Recall@10:** how often the held-out item lands in the top 10 — retrieval, not revenue.
- **LoRA (rank 16)** beat full fine-tuning in every in-domain cell.
- **Limit:** 4 of 6 transfer settings stayed at the random floor — next slide.

> Tomáš Laurin · MSc thesis, 2026 · FIT CTU
slides.group: Our Transformers and multimodal foundational models
slides.notes:
Script, 1½ min. Vojta just showed ELSA teaching a text encoder. My thesis asks two things: does the same work for a multimodal encoder — product text plus product image — and how do you measure it without fooling yourself. The measuring part is REEF: one config, several encoders, everything else pinned — same data, same chronological split, same 999 sampled negatives, same small ranker on top, same seeds. When a number moves, the encoder moved it. The table is BGE-M3 plus SigLIP2, frozen against the best adapted version: plus 16 to 29 percent Recall@10 on standard ranking, plus 14 to 39 percent on new items. Offline. The adapted version is three choices, each fixing something the frozen model gets wrong. LoRA, rank 16 on the attention projections, beat full fine-tuning in every in-domain cell — full fine-tuning even fell below frozen on new items on two of three catalogs, it damages the pretrained geometry that cold start depends on. Attention fusion conditioned on the item's co-interacted neighbours, so text and image are weighted per item instead of at one global ratio; that is the last 7 to 11 percent. And ELSA as the training signal — the same linear loss from two slides ago — beat BPR, InfoNCE and explicit item–item similarity targets on every catalog. Cost: every run fitted on one RTX 5090 with gradient checkpointing, and serving does not change — item vectors are still computed once per item, the ranker on top is the same. Recall@10 is retrieval, not revenue; validate online.

⏱ 9:37:30 · 1½ min — REEF: pin everything, vary only the encoder. Read one row: H&M 0.164 → 0.211 Recall@10, +28.7 %, new items +23.4 %. Three choices: LoRA over full tuning (full tuning damages cold start), fusion conditioned on co-interacted neighbours, ELSA as the loss — Vojta's slide, two back. One RTX 5090; serving unchanged. If behind: the table and the last bullet only. Next: what did not hold.
slides.title: Colleague spotlight: when adapting a model actually helps (Tomáš L.)
slides.summary: Laurin 2026, REEF: same data, split, negatives and ranker for every encoder. LoRA + neighbour-conditioned attention fusion + ELSA lifts BGE-M3 + SigLIP2 by +16–29 % Recall@10 offline; full fine-tuning and plain BPR do worse than the frozen encoder.

slides.body:
> Behaviour can improve multimodal encoders for ranking.

- Testing was done on three catalogs with offline evaluation
- **What improved:** in-domain results. **+16–29% Recall@10** for standard items and **+14–39%** on new items.
- **What did not:** transfer resuts: **4 of 6** held-out domains and catalog transfers remained at the random floor.
- **Why**: Held-out domains were chosen in the beggining to be difficult - it turned out, they were too difficult
- **Lessons learned**.
  - A well chosen encoder gets you most of the way, choose the right model and modalities for the task.
  - Tune with LoRA, before trying full fine tuning.
  - If you try transfer earning, analyze the overlap of the datasets.
slides.group: Our Transformers and multimodal foundational models
slides.notes:
Script, 1½ min. Now the part this room asks about first: transfer mostly failed. Six transfer cells — a held-out domain inside each catalog, and a whole held-out catalog. Four of six sat at the random-ranker floor, Recall@10 of 0.01 to 0.03 against 0.01 for a random ranking, and fine-tuning did not lift them. The UMAP projections say why. H&M swimwear and Amazon toys are islands in the embedding space, disjoint from everything the model trained on; MovieLens horror and thriller are mixed into the other genres, and that is the one domain transfer that worked, 0.21. So before you expect transfer, look at whether the target sits inside the space you trained on. Three more things that did not hold. Updating every weight was worse than LoRA in every in-domain cell and below the frozen encoder on new items on two of three catalogs. A plain BPR pairwise loss as the tuning signal made the encoder worse than frozen on two of three catalogs — the sparse signal does not constrain the geometry. Combining ELSA with InfoNCE in one loss cost 18 to 20 percent Recall@10 against the frozen encoder on both backbones; the two signals fight. And modality is a property of the catalog: a self-supervised vision encoder on movie posters scored below random ID vectors, while on fashion the image encoders led. Five times the text-encoder parameters bought between minus 8 and plus 11 percent, depending on the catalog. All of this is offline, one target against 999 sampled negatives, three English catalogs, two multimodal backbones. Nothing here is a production result.

⏱ 9:39 · 1½ min — Transfer: 4 of 6 cells at the random floor, tuned or not; the UMAP says why — the held-out domains are islands, MovieLens genres overlap, and that is the one that worked. Then three misses: full tuning, plain BPR, ELSA + InfoNCE. Modality follows the catalog: DINOv2 below random IDs on posters. Say the last line: offline, sampled negatives, English catalogs. If behind: the figure and the quote line. Bridge: offline recall is a gate, not the outcome — the scorecard next.
slides.title: Colleague spotlight: where the gains stopped (Tomáš L.)
slides.summary: The negative results from Laurin 2026: transfer sat at the random floor in 4 of 6 cells because the held-out domains are islands in the embedding space; full fine-tuning, plain BPR and a joint ELSA + InfoNCE loss did worse than the frozen encoder; modality and model size follow the catalog.

slides.body:
| Question | What to measure |
|---|---|
| **Does it help customers?** | Successful discovery, conversion or retention in A/B tests |
| **Can customers steer it?** | Whether explicit requests change results appropriately |
| **Can it fail safely?** | Invalid items, policy violations, data leakage, unauthorized actions |
| **Who gets discovered?** | Catalogue coverage and supplier exposure |
| **Can we afford it?** | Cost per successful outcome; peak-load and tail latency |

> Choose one primary business outcome and explicit guardrails before launch.
slides.notes:
Replace abstract alignment language with a release checklist owned jointly by product and engineering. Offline relevance, safety and serving metrics are useful gates, but they do not substitute for measuring customer outcomes.

⏱ 9:39 · 1 min — Alignment as five measurable properties, each with a metric and a component. Read the property column only; the next slides are the rows.
slides.title: The launch scorecard: more than clicks
slides.summary: Q8 opener: for an engineer, alignment is not a model's mood; it is five properties, each with a metric and a mechanism, each with a production example.

![[fig-shield|105%]]

**SHIELD · Recombee Labs · UMAP 2025**

Search that understands meaning can find harmful requests that keyword rules miss.

<!-- col -->

| Marketplace test: harmful vs sensitive queries | Accuracy |
|---|---|
| Keyword similarity | **93.2%** |
| Semantic search baseline | **96.5%** |
| Fine-tuned classifier | **98.4%** |

Test set: **17,170 harmful + 8,871 sensitive queries**.

> This is one classification test—not a guarantee of overall system safety.
slides.notes:
The business issue is preventing prohibited discovery without blocking legitimate customers. Ask for false-positive and false-negative rates on your own catalogue, languages and policies—not just an overall accuracy number.

⏱ 9:40 · 1 min — Semantic search walked around the keyword filter — 'glass tubing'. SHIELD: generated queries, reward-model filter, classifier, 98.4%. Ours, UMAP 2025.
slides.title: Smarter search also needs smarter safeguards
slides.summary: Semantic search understands meaning, so harmful queries walk around keyword filters; SHIELD is the dataset and classifier that closes the gap.

slides.body:
![[fig-feedback-loop|105%]]

<!-- col -->

**The feedback loop:** show popular items → collect more clicks on them → rank them higher again.

| Business risk | Countermeasure |
|---|---|
| New inventory stays invisible | Track discovery and catalogue coverage |
| A few suppliers dominate exposure | Measure supplier exposure |
| Short-term clicks narrow customer choice | Test diversity and longer-term outcomes |

Recombee research: **minimum exposure for eligible items**, with a measured relevance trade-off.

[Exposure guarantees, 2024](https://www.recombee.com/blog/making-recommendations-fairer-a-new-way-to-guarantee-exposure-for-all)
slides.notes:
For marketplaces, ranking is also allocation of commercial opportunity. Exposure floors are a policy choice with trade-offs, not a free improvement to every metric.

⏱ 9:41 · ½ min — The model learns only from what it showed; the loop amplifies popularity and hurts minority users most. Exposure is a resource — put a floor under it (ours, with a measured trade-off). Half a minute.
slides.title: Your ranking decides which suppliers get a chance (Rodrigo)
slides.summary: The model learns only from what it showed; the loop amplifies popularity, shrinks coverage and hurts minority users most; exposure guarantees are the engineering answer.

slides.body:
An off-the-shelf LLM judge can argue for **opposite engagement outcomes using identical evidence** ([Ziabari et al., 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11493)).

| Evidence | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Fluent explanation | The output sounds plausible |
| Offline evaluation | Performance on a defined test set |
| Calibrated simulation | A prediction checked against real outcomes |
| Online A/B test | The effect on your selected product metrics |

**Reported result:** behaviorally trained judging improved MacroF1 by **32.19%**, matching a production feature-based model—not proving revenue lift.

> Use AI judges to accelerate testing, not to certify their own success.

<!-- col -->

![[fig-circular-evaluation|130%]]
slides.notes:
The investor and founder takeaway is to ask what evidence sits behind an AI performance claim. Choose the experiment and success criteria before seeing the demo results.

⏱ 9:41:30 · ½ min — A zero-shot LLM judge argues both ways on the same evidence; aligned to behaviour it matches the production model. Anything between offline and A/B must be calibrated against real outcomes. Half a minute.
slides.title: A convincing AI demo is not a business experiment
slides.summary: Off-the-shelf LLM judges argue convincingly for both outcomes on the same evidence; fine-tuning with preference optimisation over correct and counterfactual rationales fixes it and matches a production feature baseline.

> Prepare trustworthy catalogue data and safe APIs—not just better chatbot copy.
slides.notes:
Treat agent commerce as a direction, not a settled protocol race or guaranteed channel shift. The low-regret investment is clean catalogue data, reliable availability and permissioned actions.
